prompt.context: Our client is a regional electricity monopoly. Due to regulation, its market will be opened to competition next year on January 1. There are no actual competitors at this time; however, the client would like ideas on actions to take in the short-term in order to better prepare for potential competitors. They have no control over pricing and cost-cutting during this time period.
prompt.question: What actions should Central Power take in the short-term to prepare for potential competitors entering its market?

clarifying_info.q: Do we know of any potential competitors?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Central Power is facing the threat of market entry.

clarifying_info.q: Do you have any information on pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Not really; pricing is controlled by a government, so it is beyond our control and will be the same for any competition.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other markets Central Power can enter?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Our engagement is focused on their home market.
Central Power has three divisions: 1. Sales and General Administration, 2. Generation and Transmission, 3. Maintenance and Repair.

clarifying_info.q: How many employees are in sales?
Does sales/customer service treat certain customer segments differently?
If there is a power outage, does Maintenance and Repair fix industrial clients first?
clarifying_info.a: No, they dispatch in the order of the call they receive.

clarifying_info.q: Has Central Power ever advertised or had a marketing campaign?
Is Central Power undertaking any capital investment?

exhibits.title: Revenue by Customer Segment
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down Central Power's customer base into three segments — Industrial, Commercial, and Residential — showing number of customers and revenue for each segment.

framework: Customer retention is the core objective — market share is 100% so acquisition is irrelevant; the goal is to prevent churn when competition arrives
Barriers to entry: no external barriers possible (government is deregulating); focus on internal barriers — increase switching costs and commercial attractiveness
Anticipation of competitive attack: identify which customer segments a rational competitor would target first and pre-empt that attack
Market information: analyze revenue by customer segment to prioritize actions
Stakeholder reaction: assess how employees, unions, and local government will react to proposed changes

questions.prompt: Look at the exhibit. What is your reaction to this revenue data?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately notice the large differences between customer segments — especially the disproportionate revenue contribution of Industrial customers. They should observe that Industrial customers (150 clients) generate 58% of total revenue ($150M of $258M), while 100,000 Residential customers generate only 19% ($48M). This insight should drive all subsequent recommendations toward defending Industrial accounts.

math.setup: Calculate each segment's share of total revenue and revenue per customer. Total revenue = $150MM + $60MM + $48MM = $258MM.
steps: Residential Customer Equivalents of one Industrial customer: $1,000,000 / $480 = ~2,083 residential customers
Residential Customer Equivalents of one Commercial customer: $6,000 / $480 = ~13 residential customers
math.answer: One Industrial customer is worth ~2,083 Residential customers in revenue terms. Industrial (150 customers) = 58% of revenue; Commercial (10,000) = 23%; Residential (100,000) = 19%.

questions.prompt: Based on this data, if you were a competitor entering this market, which segment would you target and why?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify Industrial customers as the prime target for a new competitor — high revenue concentration in few accounts makes them easy to poach with focused sales effort, and the revenue impact of losing even one industrial customer is enormous (equivalent to losing 2,083 residential customers). This sets up the logic that Central Power must prioritize defending its Industrial accounts.

questions.prompt: What specific actions should Central Power take to improve customer retention, particularly for Industrial and Commercial customers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through Central Power's three divisions systematically and generate ideas at each. Strong candidates ask questions to uncover how the company currently operates before declaring solutions. They should cover: Sales and General Administration — sign contracts, increase credit terms, grow sales force, segment sales staff by customer type, dedicate account managers to high-value clients, simplify billing, create online account management. Generation and Transmission — build substations or redundancy for industrial reliability, partner with industrial clients on energy efficiency. Maintenance and Repair — prioritize outage repairs by customer value not call order, preposition repair equipment near industrial clusters, proactively inspect client infrastructure. Assume Central Power is decades behind: no website, paper bills, no customer segmentation, no differentiated service.

brainstorming.prompt: Generate ideas for improving customer retention at Central Power, organized by division.

categories.name: Sales and General Administration
ideas: Sign long-term customer contracts to increase switching costs
Increase credit terms / days allowable for accounts receivable for high-value clients
Increase the size of the sales force
Allocate sales staff to specific customer segments (value proposition differs by segment)
Assign dedicated account managers to high-value industrial accounts
Reduce or simplify the billing process
Create a website for customers to manage accounts online
Launch a marketing campaign to build brand loyalty before competition arrives

categories.name: Generation and Transmission
ideas: Build substations or add redundancy to improve reliability for industrial clients
Work with industrial clients to improve their energy efficiency
Offer customized power quality or reliability service tiers for industrial users

categories.name: Maintenance and Repair
ideas: Prioritize outage repair by customer value (industrial first), not by call-received order
Preposition repair equipment near clusters of industrial clients to reduce response time
Proactively visit industrial clients to inspect their infrastructure
Provide engineering advice and preventive maintenance to high-value accounts

recommendation: Central Power should focus its short-term efforts on customer retention, with all priorities biased toward Industrial customers who represent 58% of revenue from only 150 accounts

Across all three divisions — Sales, Generation, and Maintenance — the company should implement measures that deepen its relationship with Industrial and Commercial clients and raise their cost of switching to a new entrant
risks: Employee and union resistance to changes in dispatch priority (Maintenance) or sales force restructuring
Local government or regulatory pushback on differentiated service levels
Cost and execution risk of implementing new systems (contracts, website, account management) within one year before deregulation
next_steps: Analyze costs and potential ROI for each proposed customer retention initiative
Assess stakeholder reactions (employees, unions, local government) to prioritized changes
Prioritize initiatives with highest retention impact and lowest implementation cost or time for the one-year window
